subject: physiology
title: Lung Volumes, Functional Residual Capacity, and Vital Capacity

steps.tx: Pulmonary ventilation relies on dynamic changes in four primary lung volumes that do not overlap. The volume of air inspired or expired during an effortless normal quiet respiratory cycle is designated the **tidal volume**. In an average healthy adult, normal resting tidal volume measures approximately five hundred millilitres.
steps.say: Tidal volume represents the air moved in or out of the lungs during quiet breathing, averaging five hundred millilitres in healthy adults.

left.title: Tidal Volume Components
points: Total volume ~500 mL (~7 mL/kg body weight)
Alveolar ventilation portion: ~350 mL reaches gas exchange zones
Anatomical dead space portion: ~150 mL fills conducting airways

right.title: Physiological Regulation
points: Driven rhythmically by dorsal respiratory group ramp signals
Controlled via phrenic nerve activation of diaphragm
Expands significantly during strenuous physical exercise

steps.tx: Beyond normal quiet tidal breathing, significant additional gas volumes can be mobilized by forced muscular effort. The maximum volume of air that can be inhaled at the end of a normal quiet inspiration is defined as the **inspiratory reserve volume**. This reserve averages roughly three thousand millilitres in young adult males.
steps.say: Inspiratory reserve volume is the maximal extra air that can be inhaled above normal tidal peak, averaging three litres.

vis.caption: Pulmonary volume measurements and ventilatory mechanics in airflow dynamics.

steps.tx: Conversely, the maximum additional volume of air that can be forcefully exhaled at the end of a tidal expiration is the **expiratory reserve volume**. Even after the most strenuous, complete exhalation, the lungs never fully collapse because a critical volume of trapped intra-alveolar gas, known as residual volume, remains inside the thoracic cavity.
steps.say: Expiratory reserve volume is the maximum air expelled after quiet expiration, while residual volume remains trapped inside alveoli.

left.title: Expiratory Reserve Volume (ERV)
points: Approximately 1100 to 1200 mL in healthy adults
Mobilized by active contraction of abdominal and internal intercostal muscles
Can be directly measured by water spirometry

right.title: Residual Volume (RV)
points: Approximately 1200 mL in healthy young adults
Prevents complete alveolar atelectasis at end-expiration
Cannot be measured by simple spirometry alone

steps.tx: Because air remains trapped within alveoli and non-collapsible conducting airways, the **residual volume** cannot be measured using simple water or dry rolling-seal spirometry. Measuring residual volume requires indirect techniques such as helium dilution, nitrogen washout, or whole-body plethysmography, which quantifies compressible thoracic gas volume.
steps.say: Residual volume cannot be measured by simple spirometry. It requires whole-body plethysmography, helium dilution, or nitrogen washout.

nodes.label: Simple Spirometry: Measures Dynamic Gas Displacements (VT, IRV, ERV, VC)
Limitation: Cannot Evacuate or Measure Residual Gas Trapped in Lungs
Plethysmography / Helium Dilution: Quantifies Total Thoracic Gas and RV

steps.tx: Combinations of two or more static volumes constitute physiological lung capacities. The volume of gas remaining in the lungs at the end of a normal passive tidal expiration is the **functional residual capacity**. It represents the sum of the expiratory reserve volume and the residual volume, averaging twenty-four hundred millilitres.
steps.say: Functional residual capacity is the equilibrium volume of air resting in the lungs after passive quiet expiration.

rows: Resting oxygen buffer preventing blood gas oscillations
Maximal gas volume inhaled after quiet expiration
Total anatomical lung volume at maximal inflation

steps.tx: At functional residual capacity, the inward elastic recoil of the pulmonary parenchyma precisely balances the outward springing elastic recoil of the thoracic wall, making intrapleural pressure negative. Pathophysiological conditions such as pulmonary emphysema increase compliance and elevate FRC, whereas restrictive disorders and severe obesity significantly reduce resting **FRC equilibrium**.
steps.say: At resting FRC equilibrium, outward chest wall recoil balances inward lung recoil. Emphysema elevates FRC, whereas obesity and fibrosis reduce it.

rows: Loss of elastic recoil tissue allows chest wall outward expansion
Cephalad displacement of diaphragm by abdominal viscera
Reduced respiratory muscle tone and chest wall geometry collapse
Excessive mechanical load compressing chest wall and diaphragm

steps.tx: The maximal volume of air that can be expired following a maximal inspiratory effort is designated the **vital capacity**. Vital capacity equals the sum of tidal volume, inspiratory reserve volume, and expiratory reserve volume, measuring approximately four thousand six hundred millilitres in healthy young adults.
steps.say: Vital capacity is the largest possible volume exhaled after maximal inhalation, combining tidal and both reserve volumes.

vis.caption: Spirometric volume subdivisions including vital capacity and inspiratory reserve in clinical assessment.

steps.tx: Adding the residual volume to the vital capacity yields the **total lung capacity**, the greatest total volume to which the lungs can expand with the greatest inspiratory effort. When total lung capacity falls below eighty percent of predicted values, a restrictive ventilatory defect is definitively diagnosed in pulmonary function testing.
steps.say: Total lung capacity is the entire gas volume held in fully inflated lungs. Restrictive ventilatory defects decrease this value below eighty percent.

nodes.label: Total Lung Capacity (TLC = VC + RV ~ 5800 mL)
Normal Range: 80% to 120% of Predicted Population Values
Restrictive Defect: TLC < 80% with Preserved or High FEV1/FVC Ratio
Obstructive Defect: Normal or High TLC with Prominent Air Trapping (High RV)
